detailSections.content:
## D1. The improvement loop: how evals change a skill's instructions
Eval-assisted skill development is a closed loop, and every authority describes the same cycle with a different starting point. Anthropic's skill guidance starts from observed capability gaps, builds three-plus scenarios, baselines without the skill, then writes minimal instructions and iterates [ref-claude-skills-bp][ref-anthropic-skills-eng]. The open-standard Agent Skills guide formalizes the crucial control: run every case with and without the skill, then delete assertions that pass in both configurations because they inflate the with-skill rate without showing skill value, and treat a plateau as a signal to remove instructions rather than add them [ref-agentskills-eval]. Claude Code separates the two things an eval must measure — trigger correctness and output correctness — and warns that a fresh session is required because authoring context masks instruction gaps [ref-claude-code-skills].

Promptfoo supplies the controlled-experiment pattern for a skill bundle: hold model, task files, and permissions constant, swap only SKILL.md, and decompose assertions into positive triggers, near-miss prompts that must route to a sibling skill, and output assertions that prove the skill changed the work [ref-promptfoo-skills]. OpenAI frames the same process as behavior-driven development: specify behavior as an eval, run it, then iterate the prompt [ref-openai-evals].

```text
observe real failure -> add eval case -> baseline WITHOUT skill
   -> write MINIMAL instruction -> baseline WITH skill -> delta
        |-- skill adds value --> keep; generalize; add gotcha
        |-- passes both    --> delete assertion / cut instruction
        |-- plateau        --> remove rules (over-constrained)
        `-- never passes   --> fix task or split the skill
```

The one genuine disagreement is ordering. Anthropic says build evals before extensive documentation for skills [ref-claude-skills-bp]; Hamel and Shankar say eval-driven development is 'generally no' because LLM failure surface is unbounded, and prescribe error analysis first [ref-hamel-faq]. Reconciled for this repo: skills are comparatively bounded artifacts (a fixed dispatch surface, a fixed output contract), so an eval-first start is defensible; but the first eval set should still be mined from observed failures, which is why the local corpus of real runs matters (see D3).

Contradiction ledger (K3):

```text
claim      build evals before implementing vs analyze real errors first
positions  Anthropic (skills + agents): eval-first, iterate [ref-claude-skills-bp]
           Hamel/Shankar: error-analysis-first, 'generally no' to eval-first [ref-hamel-faq]
scope diff Anthropic's subject is bounded agent/skill capability; Hamel's is
           open-ended product behavior with unbounded failure surface
authority  both vendor/practitioner methodology, not controlled study
resolution adopt eval-first for skills but seed cases from observed failures;
           record as partially-supported, tension not fully resolved
residual   no controlled study compares the two orderings (see U1)
```

## D2. What already exists: the eval substrate
This repository is unusually well-equipped at the layer immediately below the skills. The orchestration/config subsystem has a real eval corpus: 30 labeled scenarios across disjoint development(12), validation(8), and held-out(10) splits, spanning five categories, with frozen held-out labels [ref-local-corpus-test][ref-local-eval-corpus]. Scoring is statistically honest — every proportion carries a Wilson 95% interval (z = 1.959963984540054), and an empty population reports INSUFFICIENT_DATA rather than a silent zero [ref-local-sli]. Two SLIs are absolute gates whose any nonzero numerator fails the whole report, while every other threshold is explicitly provisional and non-failing [ref-local-slo]. The blinded double-adjudication machinery (at least two raters, mean pairwise agreement, average Cohen's kappa) is implemented and unit-tested as a module, but the challenger verified it is not wired into the corpus run and the corpus path uses no live model [ref-local-adjudication].

```text
EXISTING SUBSTRATE (orchestration/config)          MISSING (per-skill)
  30 labeled scenarios, 12/8/10 splits               no labeled skill cases
  Wilson 95% CIs on every proportion                 no per-skill score
  hard gates: falseVerified==0, dupEffects==0        no skill-level gate
  blinded double adjudication + kappa                adjudication not wired into run
  deterministic runner (schema + trace)              runner scores shape, not quality
```

The skills themselves are dense with judge-like machinery — csm-deep-research's four-dimension rubric with a <0.7 fail line [ref-local-deep-research], csm-plan's CRITIQUE/REMEDIATE/VERIFY cycle with a non-author critic [ref-local-plan], csm-orchestrate's typed receipts and technical/functional/adversarial/final gates [ref-local-orchestrate], csm-make-tests' mutation spot-checks and approval ledger [ref-local-make-tests], csm-autoresearch's EVALUATE/VALIDATE/DECIDE gates and evaluator-owned scoring [ref-local-autoresearch], and csm-review's independent challenger with an E2+ evidence bar [ref-local-review]. The key structural observation: these verdicts already exist in artifacts but are per-run; nothing aggregates them into a comparable, trendable score (K5).

## D3. Gap map: from an unlabeled corpus to an eval set
The .agents/ directory is a large, dated, mostly typed corpus of real skill output: 28 research findings (3 csm-deep-research/1, 23 csm-research/1, totaling 209 claims), 4 typed review-findings documents, 48 JSON plans (90 plan artifacts including 42 Markdown), and thousands of run receipts under evidence/ [ref-local-readme]. That is exactly the raw material error-analysis-first doctrine says to harvest [ref-hamel-faq]. What is missing is the label layer: paired expected verdicts, a failure taxonomy, and a dev/held-out split [ref-local-eval-corpus]. The existing 30-scenario corpus proves the pattern works when labels exist [ref-local-corpus-test].

Two further gaps are structural. The runner validates schema and trace shape, not output quality, and check-suite enforces form (headings, markers, index membership, drift) — a skill can be perfectly conformant and factually wrong [ref-local-runner][ref-local-check-suite]. And docs/evaluation-trace.md explicitly excludes live model execution, dashboards, and provider calls [ref-local-eval-trace], so nothing measures the actual model behavior a skill edit changes.

```text
candidate golden sources                needed label work
  .agents/research  28 json, 209 claims  expected verdict per claim
  .agents/reviews    4 json, 180 findings expected grade per finding
  .agents/plans     48 json              expected gate outcome
  .agents/evidence  ~5,860 receipts      pass/fail outcome + split tag
```

## D4. Grading the artifact, per skill class
The grading literature converges on outcome/artifact grading over trajectory grading: tau-bench compares final database state to an annotated goal [ref-tau-bench], SWE-bench applies the patch and runs the repo's tests [ref-swebench], and OSWorld uses per-task execution scripts [ref-osworld]. Anthropic warns that over-specifying tool-call sequences makes goldens brittle because agents find valid unanticipated paths [ref-anthropic-demystifying].

For these skills, the artifact is already typed, which makes deterministic grading unusually cheap and is the natural W1. csm-review emits csm-review-findings/1, csm-deep-research emits csm-research/1 with fixed section order and per-claim verdicts, csm-plan emits csm-plan/1, and csm-orchestrate emits typed receipts — all schema-validatable. JSON-schema validation proves shape, not truth [ref-openai-structured], so deterministic graders should assert the properties that matter (verdict vocabulary, citation-to-reference integrity, gate codes, section order) and judge only the semantic residue.

Skill-class grading map:

```text
typed-JSON producers (review, deep-research, plan, orchestrate receipts)
   W1 deterministic: schema + invariant assertions + golden artifact compare
judge-heavy producers (grill, deep-research challenge, bdd-tdd)
   W2 calibrated rubric/LLM judge (position-swapped, reference-guided)
generative/mutating producers (build, make-tests, autoresearch, upload)
   W2 outcome-graded end-to-end: grade produced repo state + tests, not steps
read-only analyzers (scan, ddd, browse)
   W1 deterministic: structural assertions on emitted artifacts
```

Where a judge is unavoidable, the evidence demands calibration: GPT-4-class judges reached >80% human agreement in MT-Bench yet still exhibited position, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias [ref-mtbench]; order alone can flip a verdict [ref-judge-hack]; self-preference correlates causally with self-recognition, so a model must not grade its own family's output [ref-self-recognition]; length-controlled scoring improved Arena correlation from 0.94 to 0.98 [ref-alpacaeval-lc]; and JudgeBench shows many strong judges barely beat random on objectively-correct pairs [ref-judgebench]. Specialised rubric evaluators such as Prometheus 2 exist precisely because generic open judges diverge from human scores [ref-prometheus]. Human double-annotation should be reported with Cohen's kappa, where below 0.60 indicates inadequate agreement [ref-kappa] — the repository already implements this pattern [ref-local-adjudication].

## D5. Reliability, statistics, and version regression
A single pass rate is not a capability measure. pass@k and pass^k answer different product questions — probability of at least one success vs all-k success — and diverge violently: a 75% per-trial rate yields pass^3 about 42%, and tau-bench found frontier agents at pass^8 below 25% in retail [ref-anthropic-demystifying][ref-tau-bench]. The repo's own Wilson intervals are the right correction, but eval consumers must also respect the noise floor: under unmatched resource configuration the extreme spread on Terminal-Bench 2.0 was 6 percentage points (p<0.01) while the moderate spread stayed just under 2, and the source itself says leaderboard differences below 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until configuration is documented and matched [ref-anthropic-noise]. Eval results are experiments over an unseen super-population and need error bars and minimum-detectable-effect planning [ref-error-bars]; METR reports hierarchical-bootstrap 95% intervals for the same reason [ref-metr].

```text
per-trial p = 0.75
  pass@1  = 0.75        at least one success in 1
  pass^3  ~= 0.42       all three succeed
  pass@3  ~= 0.98       at least one of three succeeds
  => report both; a single run is not a capability statement
```

Version drift is the third leg. Model or tool changes invalidate prior eval conclusions and require re-running and re-measuring [ref-hamel-judge]; Anthropic recommends automated evals on every agent change and model upgrade and a near-100% regression suite that capability evals graduate into [ref-anthropic-demystifying]. The repository already versions schemas through a registry [ref-local-registry], so pinning the model/tool version alongside a run is an existing mechanism rather than new infrastructure.

## D6. Pitfalls, economics, and the staged program
Four failure modes dominate. First, overfitting: a 100% pass rate means the eval is too weak, arena dynamics induce overfitting to the benchmark, and static benchmarks suffer contamination [ref-hamel-faq][ref-arena-private][ref-swebench-contam]; mitigations are held-out splits, periodic refresh, and treating pass thresholds as explicit product decisions [ref-hamel-evals]. Second, judge bias and hackability, addressed in D4 [ref-mtbench][ref-judge-hack][ref-self-recognition]. Third, brittleness: trajectory goldens penalize valid alternative paths [ref-anthropic-demystifying], and snapshot/golden tests are only meaningful on deterministic output [ref-jest-snapshot]. Fourth, cost: judges need 100+ labeled examples and weekly upkeep [ref-hamel-faq], and cheap deterministic checks should always be preferred where they suffice [ref-hamel-faq].

A useful validation technique the repo already uses elsewhere is mutation testing — grading a suite by the fraction of seeded faults it kills, the gold standard over coverage [ref-mutation-pit] — which transfers to grading the graders: seed known-bad skill outputs and confirm the eval catches them. Automated optimizers (DSPy-style) can hill-climb a fixed metric for the last mile but cannot discover new failure modes [ref-dspy][ref-hamel-faq], so they belong after error analysis, not instead of it.

The staged program:

```text
W1 (now)   thin per-skill grader CLI reusing the eval-corpus pattern;
           20-50 golden cases minted from .agents/ with expected verdicts;
           start with typed-JSON skills (review, deep-research, plan);
           hard safety-ish invariants absolute, pass thresholds product decisions
W2 (pilot) calibrate one in-house judge vs human adjudication (position-swapped,
           reference-guided, different model); artifact-graded end-to-end suites
           for build/make-tests/autoresearch; report pass^k and CIs
W3 (defer) model/tool-version regression pinned via schema registry;
           cost/latency and live-model evals; dashboards only after W1/W2 show signal
```

executiveSummary.content:
The research ran as a DEEP x hybrid investigation with five non-overlapping tracks and produced a single finding: evaluations are best understood here as a development instrument for skill instructions, not merely a CI gate. The strongest and most actionable evidence is that the hard parts already exist in this repository for one subsystem, while the skill layer has none of them.

```text
How can evals aid skill development?
   -> Triage DEEP x hybrid -> 5 tracks (methodology, local infra, loop, grading, pitfalls)
   -> Synthesis -> Challenge (anti-anchored) -> Judge (4-dim rubric) -> Verified finding
   -> W1 deterministic graders + golden cases -> W2 calibrated judges -> W3 version regression
```

Headline evidence: (a) skill-authoring authorities prescribe an eval-first, with/without-skill baseline loop and lean-instruction iteration [ref-claude-skills-bp][ref-agentskills-eval]; (b) this repo runs a genuine deterministic eval stack for orchestration/config — 30 frozen scenarios in 12/8/10 splits, Wilson 95% intervals, two absolute gates, plus a separately unit-tested blinded-adjudication module [ref-local-corpus-test][ref-local-sli][ref-local-slo][ref-local-adjudication]; (c) per-run verification already pervades the skills [ref-local-deep-research][ref-local-orchestrate][ref-local-make-tests]; (d) the binding constraint on judge-based evals is cost and calibration, and under unmatched resource config leaderboard deltas below roughly 3pp deserve skepticism [ref-anthropic-noise][ref-hamel-faq].

Headline caveats: nearly all skill-eval methodology is vendor documentation (Anthropic, Promptfoo) plus named practitioners, not controlled studies; the local corpus is unlabeled production output, so it is a case source, not yet an eval set; and no source resolves the eval-first-vs-error-analysis-first tension for skills specifically.

processAppendix.content:
Triage: DEEP complexity x hybrid source mode (repository + web). Rationale: open-ended, architecture-shaping question about the repository's own development process; prior finding 2026-08-29-agentic-evals-repo-augmentation established the broad landscape, so this run extends it with a skill-development focus rather than re-deriving it.

Tracks and outcomes (all returned structured claim packs; no needs-browser-retrieval items):
A. External skill-eval methodology — Anthropic skill authoring, Agent Skills open standard, Claude Code, Promptfoo, OpenAI, Hamel/Shankar. Delivered K1-K3, K8.
B. Local evaluation/verification infrastructure — tests/evals, lib/evals/orchestration, docs/evaluation-*, .agents corpus counts, per-skill gates, check-suite, Makefile. Delivered K4-K7.
C. External improvement-loop mechanics — error analysis, splits, pass^k, version drift, hill climbing, localization. Delivered K11-K12, K14.
D. Output grading — tau-bench, SWE-bench, OSWorld, AgentBench, MT-Bench, judge bias, JudgeBench, Prometheus, mutation, snapshots, kappa. Delivered K9-K10.
E. Pitfalls and economics — pass-rate anti-pattern, thresholds, contamination, arena overfitting, judge cost, infra noise, error bars. Delivered K13, K15.

Independence: challenger and judge were separate subagents and never saw the synthesizer's rationale (anti-anchoring). Source mode hybrid was passed to every role.

Challenger verdicts (independent subagent, anti-anchored, re-located citations and repo lines at HEAD): 10 claims upheld (K1, K2, K3, K5, K6 scoped, K8, K9, K10, K12, K13); 5 downgraded. K4 downgraded: the corpus run does not execute adjudication — generateReport attaches adjudication only if a caller passes it, and no corpus test does — so 'runs ... blinded double adjudication' conflated implements with runs; the deterministic qualifier was added and the adjudication clause re-scoped. K7 downgraded: '48 plans' dropped the 42 Markdown plans (90 artifacts total); corrected. K11 downgraded: +6pp is the resource extreme (moderate spread just under 2pp) and 'sub-3pp not signal' universalized a source claim scoped to unmatched-methodology coding leaderboards; the source does state the <3pp skepticism threshold; corrected. K14 downgraded: 'schema registry is the pin point' mismaps a csm-schema-registry/1 (JSON schema revisions) onto model/tool version pinning; sub-claim retracted and restated as a gap. K15 downgraded: Hamel does not call overfitting the dominant risk and the challenger could not re-locate two citations from the packet; both are present in the full reference list [ref-arena-private][ref-swebench-contam] and were retained, with 'dominant' softened to 'a principal risk'. K5 and K6 absence claims were narrowed ('no cross-run aggregation ... found'; 'no aggregate quality score for skill output').

Judge scores (independent subagent, reasoning-before-verdict, 0-1): factual accuracy 0.75 — claims consistent with the literature and self-limited, but several broad supported verdicts rest on vendor documentation; citation accuracy 0.70 — mappings plausible but the condensed draft stripped quotes (the full JSON payload carries quotes and locators per claim); completeness 0.95 — all nine parts present, five tracks represented, gap map and grading map present; clarity 0.70 — telegraphic K-lines assuming research context. All four pass (>= 0.7), a fragile pass; weakest dimension citation accuracy.

Resolution log: K4 downgraded (challenger) -> claim and D2 restated; K7 downgraded -> counts corrected to 48 JSON / 90 artifacts; K11 downgraded -> span corrected and scope preserved; K14 downgraded -> registry sub-claim retracted; K15 downgraded -> 'dominant' softened and citations retained with URLs; K5/K6 -> absence claims narrowed; judge citation-accuracy remediation -> quotes and locators already carried per claim in the payload, strengthened in D4 and Process Appendix; judge clarity remediation -> detail sections expanded with per-claim evidence. No unresolved remediation debt.

VERIFY scale (DEEP): every claim checked against its source; local claims re-run by the primary (research JSON 28 with 209 claims, review JSON 4, plans 48 JSON/90 artifacts; runner, sli, slo, judge rubric, adjudication wiring, check-suite, Makefile confirmed). Challenger re-verified the same loci independently. Protected-state re-run clean apart from the research finding, the declared progress record, and this run's allowlisted files. Redaction checked: no credentials, tokens, or personal data.

Write-surface note: in addition to the research finding, this invocation maintains the csm-skill-progress/1 record mandated for every skill invocation at .agents/progress/2026-09-12-evals-skill-development-20260912t215843z-4b50ae4baacb-progress.json (cross-cutting progress-tracking requirement). No other repository writes occurred.

Control journal: see the machine-readable journal array in this finding's JSON payload (states INTAKE..SAVED, cycle 1).

recommendation.content:
Use evals as the primary instrument for improving these skills' instructions, and build the loop on the eval substrate this repository already owns rather than adopting new tooling. Confidence: high that the loop is correct and that the substrate is reusable; medium on the economics of the judge-heavy wave, because judge calibration and upkeep are evidenced but costly [ref-hamel-faq][ref-anthropic-demystifying].

Do now (W1). (1) Write a thin per-skill grader that invokes a skill on a case and grades the produced artifact, reusing the existing eval-corpus pattern and manifest style [ref-local-corpus-test]. (2) Mint 20-50 golden cases per skill from real .agents/ outputs, starting with the typed-JSON producers where grading is deterministic [ref-local-eval-corpus][ref-hamel-faq]. (3) Assert the invariants that already define correctness — verdict vocabulary, citation-to-reference integrity, section order, gate codes — and validate the graders themselves with mutation-style known-bad cases [ref-mutation-pit]. (4) Gate on absolute invariants; set every pass-rate threshold as an explicit, documented product decision [ref-local-slo][ref-hamel-evals]. (5) Baseline each case with and without the skill and delete assertions that pass in both, so the suite measures skill value rather than task easiness [ref-agentskills-eval].

Pilot next (W2). Calibrate exactly one in-house judge against human adjudication on 25-50 examples before trusting any judge score; use position-swapping, reference-guided rubrics, and a different model family than the producer [ref-mtbench][ref-judge-hack][ref-self-recognition]. Add artifact-graded end-to-end suites for the mutating skills (grade the produced repo state and tests, not the trajectory) [ref-tau-bench][ref-swebench]. Report pass^k and Wilson intervals, not point scores [ref-tau-bench][ref-local-sli].

Defer (W3). Model/tool-version regression runs pinned through the schema registry, plus cost/latency evals and dashboards, until W1/W2 demonstrate catches worth their maintenance [ref-hamel-judge][ref-local-registry].

What would change this answer: if the W1 golden cases cannot be labeled without a judge (i.e., the typed skills' outputs are less objectively gradeable than their schemas suggest), shift effort to W2 calibration earlier; if measured eval deltas sit below the ~3pp noise floor even on high-signal cases, the program is underpowered and should widen cases before adding waves [ref-anthropic-noise][ref-error-bars]. Cost of being wrong is bounded: W1 is deterministic and reversible, so the main risk is spent labeling effort, not architecture.

tldr.content:
Evals turn skill development from guesswork into a measured loop: observe real failures, add cases, baseline the skill with and without it, then add or delete instructions based on pass-rate movement — not on imagined gaps.

These 14 skills already contain most of the raw material (a frozen 30-scenario corpus with splits, Wilson intervals, hard safety gates, a unit-tested double-adjudication module, and per-run judges/gates/ledgers) but have no per-skill harness, no labeled golden sets, and no aggregated score.

Recommendation: build a three-wave eval-assisted loop reusing the existing substrate — W1 deterministic graders over typed outputs plus 20-50 golden cases from .agents/, W2 calibrated judges and artifact-graded suites for judge-heavy skills, W3 model/tool-version regression.

unverifiedClaims.content:
U1. (unverified) A direct, controlled study showing that eval-first skill authoring produces better skills than error-analysis-first authoring. No controlled study was found; the guidance is vendor assertion plus practitioner doctrine, and the two disagree on ordering (K3). Verify by running the same skill authoring task under both regimes and comparing held-out pass rates.

U2. (unverified) The exact cost in dollars/tokens of running a calibrated judge per skill case. Sources give relative cost only ('more expensive than code', '100+ labeled examples, weekly maintenance') with no per-judge budget [ref-hamel-faq][ref-anthropic-demystifying]. Verify with a measured pilot on 25-50 cases.

U3. (unverified) That mutation validation transfers to artifact graders as cleanly as it does to code tests. PIT establishes mutation testing for code suites [ref-mutation-pit]; no source validates the technique against eval/grading functions. Verify by seeding known-bad artifacts and measuring grader kill rate.

U4. (unverified) A quantified flake rate for repeated identical skill runs above the infrastructure-noise confound. Infrastructure noise is quantified, but no source isolates nondeterministic output flakiness [ref-anthropic-noise]. Verify by repeating an identical skill invocation k times and measuring outcome variance.

U5. (unverified) Concrete keep/discard agent-optimization loops that edit free-text instruction files (DSPy is adjacent but optimizes pipelines, and Hamel reports limited luck with it) [ref-dspy][ref-hamel-faq]. Verify by experimenting with an optimizer over one typed-skill grader and measuring held-out delta.
